summary.text: Writing each rank as \(n+\lfloor e^{H_n}-1\rfloor\), the proof establishes \(1<e^{H_{n+1}}-e^{H_n}<2\) using elementary exponential inequalities, monotonicity of \(e^{H_n}/n\), and explicit Taylor bounds for the finitely many initial cases; the resulting floor increment is therefore 1 or 2. Telescoping gives exact formulas for the counts of the two step sizes, and \(H_n-\log n\to\gamma\) makes their ratio tend to \((e^\gamma-1)/(2-e^\gamma)\); harmonic-sum and logarithm estimates at 512 and 1024, together with Taylor bounds for the exponential, show \(16/9<e^\gamma<41/23\), placing this limit strictly between 3.5 and 3.6.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
H_n=\sum_{j=1}^n\frac1j\qquad(n\geq 1),
\]
and let \(a(n)\) be the position of \(H_n\) when the numbers \(H_1,H_2,\ldots\) and \(\log 2,\log 3,\ldots\) are put into one increasing list.

We first obtain a convenient exact formula for this rank. The harmonic sums are strictly increasing, so the harmonic terms at or before \(H_n\) are exactly \(H_1,\ldots,H_n\), contributing \(n\) positions. Moreover,
\[
\log(k+1)<H_n\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad k<e^{H_n}-1.
\]
There are therefore \(\lfloor e^{H_n}-1\rfloor\) logarithmic terms before \(H_n\), provided that \(e^{H_n}-1\) is not an integer. There are indeed no ties: \(H_n\) is a nonzero rational number, and the Hermite–Lindemann theorem says that the exponential of a nonzero algebraic number is transcendental. Thus \(e^{H_n}\), in particular, is not an integer. Consequently
\[
\boxed{a(n)=n+\lfloor e^{H_n}-1\rfloor.}\tag{1}
\]
This also directly gives \(a(1)=2\), since \(H_1=1\) and \(1<e-1<2\).

We next prove the central estimate
\[
\boxed{1<e^{H_{n+1}}-e^{H_n}<2\qquad(n\geq1).}\tag{2}
\]
Since
\[
H_{n+1}=H_n+\frac1{n+1},
\]
we have
\[
e^{H_{n+1}}-e^{H_n}
=e^{H_n}\left(e^{1/(n+1)}-1\right).\tag{3}
\]

For the lower bound, first note that
\[
e^{H_n}>n+1\qquad(n\geq1).\tag{4}
\]
This follows by induction. At \(n=1\), it is the familiar inequality \(e>2\). If it holds at \(n\), then the strict inequality \(e^x>1+x\) for \(x>0\) gives
\[
e^{H_{n+1}}
=e^{H_n}e^{1/(n+1)}
>(n+1)\left(1+\frac1{n+1}\right)=n+2.
\]
Applying \(e^x-1>x\) once more in (3), and using (4), yields
\[
e^{H_{n+1}}-e^{H_n}
>e^{H_n}\frac1{n+1}>1.
\]
This proves the left side of (2).

For the upper bound we use, for every \(n\geq1\),
\[
e^{1/(n+1)}<1+\frac1n.\tag{5}
\]
Indeed, apply \(e^x>1+x\) to \(x=-1/(n+1)\). This gives
\[
e^{-1/(n+1)}>1-\frac1{n+1}=\frac n{n+1}.
\]
Both sides are positive, so taking reciprocals reverses the inequality and gives
\[
e^{1/(n+1)}<\frac{n+1}{n}=1+\frac1n.
\]
It follows that the sequence
\[
q_n=\frac{e^{H_n}}n
\]
is strictly decreasing, because
\[
q_{n+1}
=\frac{e^{H_n}e^{1/(n+1)}}{n+1}
<\frac{e^{H_n}(1+1/n)}{n+1}
=\frac{e^{H_n}}n=q_n.\tag{6}
\]
Now
\[
H_5=1+\frac12+\frac13+\frac14+\frac15=\frac{137}{60},
\]
and an explicit exponential estimate gives
\[
e^{137/60}<10.\tag{7}
\]
For completeness, this estimate can be obtained without decimal approximation as follows. Write \(137/60=3(137/180)\). For
\[
P_3(x)=1+x+\frac{x^2}{2}+\frac{x^3}{6},
\]
the Taylor remainder estimate used here is
\[
|e^x-P_3(x)|\leq \frac{|x|^4}{4!}\frac54
\]
for the positive rational arguments in question. At \(x=137/180\),
\[
P_3(x)=\frac{74331413}{34992000}.
\]
Direct rational arithmetic shows that the displayed remainder is less than \(18/1000\), while the polynomial value is less than \(21251/10000\). Hence \(e^{137/180}<215/100\), and therefore
\[
e^{137/60}=\left(e^{137/180}\right)^3
<\left(\frac{215}{100}\right)^3<10,
\]
proving (7).

By (6) and (7), for every \(n\geq5\),
\[
\frac{e^{H_n}}n\leq \frac{e^{H_5}}5<2.
\]
Combining this with (3) and (5),
\[
e^{H_{n+1}}-e^{H_n}
<e^{H_n}\frac1n<2
\qquad(n\geq5).\tag{8}
\]

It remains to check \(n=1,2,3,4\). The following rational bounds suffice:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\frac{27}{10}<e^{H_1}<\frac{28}{10},\\
&\frac{44}{10}<e^{H_2}<\frac{45}{10},\\
&\frac{611}{100}<e^{H_3}<\frac{63}{10},\\
&8<e^{H_4}<\frac{805}{100},\\
&e^{H_5}<10.
\end{aligned}\tag{9}
\]
They immediately imply
\[
\begin{aligned}
e^{H_2}-e^{H_1}&<4.5-2.7<2,\\
e^{H_3}-e^{H_2}&<6.3-4.4<2,\\
e^{H_4}-e^{H_3}&<8.05-6.11<2,\\
e^{H_5}-e^{H_4}&<10-8<2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here are details establishing the less standard bounds in (9). We have
\[
H_2=\frac32,\qquad H_3=\frac{11}{6},\qquad H_4=\frac{25}{12}.
\]
For \(H_2\), apply the same cubic Taylor estimate to \(x=1/2\). Since
\[
P_3(1/2)=\frac{79}{48},\qquad
\frac{(1/2)^4}{4!}\frac54=\frac5{1536},
\]
we obtain
\[
\frac{2523}{1536}\leq e^{1/2}\leq\frac{2533}{1536}.
\]
Cubing these rational bounds, because \(e^{H_2}=(e^{1/2})^3\), gives
\[
\frac{44}{10}<e^{H_2}<\frac{45}{10}.
\]
For \(H_3\), put \(x=11/18\). Then
\[
P_3(x)=\frac{64241}{34992},
\qquad
\frac{x^4}{4!}\frac54=\frac{73205}{10077696},
\]
so
\[
\frac{18428203}{10077696}\leq e^{11/18}
\leq\frac{18574613}{10077696}.
\]
Cubing and comparing rational numbers gives
\[
\frac{611}{100}<e^{11/6}<\frac{63}{10}.
\]
For the upper bound at \(H_4\), put \(x=25/36\). Here
\[
P_3(x)=\frac{557461}{279936},
\qquad
\frac{x^4}{4!}\frac54=\frac{1953125}{161243136},
\]
whence
\[
e^{25/36}\leq\frac{323050661}{161243136}.
\]
Cubing gives \(e^{25/12}<805/100\). For the lower bound, write
\[
\frac{25}{12}=1+1+\frac1{12}.
\]
The elementary estimates
\[
e>\frac{2718281828}{10^9},\qquad e^{1/12}>1+\frac1{12}
\]
give
\[
e^{25/12}>
\left(\frac{2718281828}{10^9}\right)^2\left(1+\frac1{12}\right)>8.
\]
Finally, \(2.7<e<2.8\), obtainable from the ordinary exponential series with a geometric bound on its positive tail, gives the bounds at \(H_1\). Thus (9) is established, and together with (8) proves (2) for all \(n\geq1\).

We now transfer (2) to the floor terms in (1). We use the elementary floor lemma:

If real numbers \(x,y\) satisfy \(1<x-y<2\), then
\[
\lfloor x\rfloor-\lfloor y\rfloor\in\{1,2\}.\tag{10}
\]
Indeed, from \(x<\lfloor x\rfloor+1\) and \(\lfloor y\rfloor\leq y\), the inequality \(x-y>1\) implies
\(
\lfloor x\rfloor-\lfloor y\rfloor>0.
\)
Similarly, \(\lfloor x\rfloor\leq x\) and \(y<\lfloor y\rfloor+1\), together with \(x-y<2\), imply
\(
\lfloor x\rfloor-\lfloor y\rfloor<3.
\)
This difference is an integer, so it is \(1\) or \(2\).

Take
\[
x=e^{H_{n+1}}-1,
\qquad y=e^{H_n}-1.
\]
By (2), the hypotheses of (10) hold. Formula (1) therefore gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(n+1)-a(n)
&=1+\lfloor e^{H_{n+1}}-1\rfloor
      -\lfloor e^{H_n}-1\rfloor\\
&\in\{2,3\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves the first assertion of the conjecture.

We turn to the ratio assertion. For \(N\geq0\), let \(C_3(N)\) and \(C_2(N)\) denote, respectively, the numbers of 3's and 2's among
\[
a(2)-a(1),\ a(3)-a(2),\ldots,\ a(N+1)-a(N).
\]
There are exactly \(N\) differences, and all are 2 or 3, so
\[
C_2(N)+C_3(N)=N.\tag{11}
\]
Moreover, subtracting 2 from each difference turns a 2 into 0 and a 3 into 1. Hence telescoping gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
C_3(N)
&=\sum_{n=1}^N\bigl(a(n+1)-a(n)-2\bigr)\\
&=a(N+1)-a(1)-2N.
\end{aligned}
\]
Using (1) and \(a(1)=2\), we obtain the exact formulas
\[
\boxed{C_3(N)=\lfloor e^{H_{N+1}}-1\rfloor-N-1,}\tag{12}
\]
\[
\boxed{C_2(N)=2N+1-\lfloor e^{H_{N+1}}-1\rfloor.}\tag{13}
\]

Let \(\gamma\) denote the Euler–Mascheroni constant. The classical harmonic-number limit is
\[
H_n-\log n\longrightarrow\gamma.
\]
Exponentiating and using \(e^{\log n}=n\) gives
\[
\frac{e^{H_n}}n=e^{H_n-\log n}\longrightarrow e^\gamma.
\]
Replacing \(n\) by \(N+1\), and observing that \((N+1)/N\to1\), yields
\[
\frac{e^{H_{N+1}}}{N}\longrightarrow e^\gamma.\tag{14}
\]
The floor does not affect this limit. Indeed, for every real \(t\),
\[
t-1<\lfloor t\rfloor\leq t.
\]
With \(t=e^{H_{N+1}}-1\), division by \(N>0\) gives
\[
\frac{e^{H_{N+1}}-2}{N}
<\frac{\lfloor e^{H_{N+1}}-1\rfloor}{N}
\leq\frac{e^{H_{N+1}}-1}{N}.
\]
Both outer terms tend to \(e^\gamma\) by (14), so
\[
\frac{\lfloor e^{H_{N+1}}-1\rfloor}{N}\longrightarrow e^\gamma.\tag{15}
\]
Dividing (12) and (13) by \(N\), and using (15), gives
\[
\frac{C_3(N)}N\longrightarrow e^\gamma-1,
\qquad
\frac{C_2(N)}N\longrightarrow 2-e^\gamma.\tag{16}
\]
We will shortly show \(e^\gamma<2\), so the second limit is nonzero. It then follows from (16) that
\[
\boxed{
\frac{C_3(N)}{C_2(N)}\longrightarrow
L:=\frac{e^\gamma-1}{2-e^\gamma}.}
\tag{17}
\]

It remains to prove the required strict numerical bounds on \(L\). We establish the sharper rational bounds
\[
\boxed{\frac{16}{9}<e^\gamma<\frac{41}{23}.}\tag{18}
\]
We include the explicit estimates.

The standard integral comparison for harmonic sums gives, for every positive integer \(m\),
\[
H_m-\log(m+1)<\gamma<H_m-\log m.\tag{19}
\]
For the lower estimate take \(m=512\). Exact summation of the rational numbers \(1,1/2,\ldots,1/512\), after putting them over a common denominator, gives
\[
H_{512}>\frac{68165}{10000}.
\]
Also
\[
\log513=\log512+\log\frac{513}{512}
=9\log2+\log\left(1+\frac1{512}\right).
\]
Since \(\log(1+u)\leq u\) for \(u>-1\),
\[
\log513\leq9\log2+\frac1{512}.
\]
The rational estimate
\[
\log2<0.6931471808
\]
therefore shows, by direct rational subtraction, that
\[
H_{512}-\log513>\frac{576}{1000}.
\]
By (19),
\[
\gamma>\frac{576}{1000}.\tag{20}
\]

For the upper estimate take \(m=1024\). Exact rational summation gives
\[
H_{1024}<\frac{75092}{10000}.
\]
Since \(1024=2^{10}\),
\[
\log1024=10\log2.
\]
Using
\[
\log2>0.6931471803
\]
and again doing the indicated rational subtraction gives
\[
H_{1024}-\log1024<\frac{578}{1000}.
\]
Thus (19) gives
\[
\gamma<\frac{578}{1000}.\tag{21}
\]
The two displayed bounds for \(\log2\) can, for example, be proved entirely rationally from
\[
\log2=2\left(\frac13+\frac{1}{3\cdot3^3}+\frac{1}{5\cdot3^5}+\cdots\right),
\]
obtained by integrating the geometric series for \((1-t^2)^{-1}\) from \(0\) to \(1/3\). Truncating this positive series gives the lower bound, and bounding its remaining terms by a geometric tail gives the upper bound. Thus the decimal notation above represents exact rational inequalities, not numerical assumptions.

We now exponentiate (20)–(21). The needed endpoint estimates are
\[
\frac{16}{9}<e^{576/1000},
\qquad
e^{578/1000}<\frac{41}{23}.\tag{22}
\]
These follow from the sixth-order rational Taylor bounds. More explicitly, let
\[
P_5(x)=\sum_{j=0}^5\frac{x^j}{j!}.
\]
For each of the two positive arguments under consideration,
\[
|e^x-P_5(x)|
\leq\frac{x^6}{6!}\frac76.\tag{23}
\]
At \(x=576/1000\), exact evaluation gives
\[
P_5(x)=\frac{271431477193}{152587890625}.
\]
Consequently (23) gives
\[
e^{576/1000}\geq
\frac{271431477193}{152587890625}
-\frac{(576/1000)^6}{720}\frac76.
\]
Cross-multiplication of positive integers shows that the right side is greater than \(16/9\).
At \(x=578/1000\),
\[
P_5(x)=\frac{6684050732502949}{3750000000000000},
\]
and (23) gives
\[
e^{578/1000}\leq
\frac{6684050732502949}{3750000000000000}
+\frac{(578/1000)^6}{720}\frac76.
\]
Another direct cross-multiplication shows that this right side is less than \(41/23\). This proves (22). Since the exponential is strictly increasing, (20), (21), and (22) imply (18).

In particular \(e^\gamma<41/23<2\), as required in passing from (16) to (17). Finally, because \(2-e^\gamma>0\), the lower bound in (18) gives
\[
\frac{e^\gamma-1}{2-e^\gamma}>\frac72
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
2(e^\gamma-1)>7(2-e^\gamma)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
e^\gamma>\frac{16}{9}.
\]
Likewise, the upper bound in (18) gives
\[
\frac{e^\gamma-1}{2-e^\gamma}<\frac{18}{5}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
5(e^\gamma-1)<18(2-e^\gamma)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
e^\gamma<\frac{41}{23}.
\]
Therefore
\[
3.5< L <3.6,
\qquad
L=\frac{e^\gamma-1}{2-e^\gamma},
\]
and (17) says precisely that the ratio of the number of 3's to the number of 2's among the first \(N\) successive differences tends to this \(L\). Together with the earlier proof that every difference is 2 or 3, this proves both parts of the conjecture.
